**Lu Xun – author of “Diary of a Madman” and “The True Story of Ah Q.”**  
Lu Xun is the founding figure of modern Chinese literature; his short stories are standard clues for China because they are frequently cited in quizbowl as the first major works of the 20th‑century “New Culture” movement.

**Liu Cixin – writer of “The Three‑Body Problem” and “The Dark Forest.”**  
Liu’s hard‑science‑fiction trilogy, featuring the alien civilization Trisolaris, is a signature contemporary Chinese author that appears in many literary‑science clues.

**Journey to the West (Xi You Ji) – the Monkey‑King novel.**  
The classic tale of Sun Wukong, Pigsy, Sandy and the monk Tripitaka is one of the Four Great Classical Novels and is repeatedly referenced through its characters, magical staff, and pilgrimage plot.

**The Four Great Classical Novels – Water Margin, Dream of the Red Chamber, Journey to the West, Romance of the Three Kingdoms.**  
These four works are a staple identifier for Chinese literary culture; any mention of one of them usually signals China.

**Tang‑Dynasty poets Du Fu, Li Bai, and Wang Wei.**  
These poets are the most famous representatives of Tang poetry; clues citing “Quiet Night Thought,” “Drinking Alone by Moonlight,” or “Song of the Wagons” point directly to China.

**Gao Xingjian – Nobel‑winning playwright and author of “Soul Mountain.”**  
Gao’s exile‑inspired novel and his Nobel Prize in Literature are hallmark modern‑Chinese cultural references.

**Mo Yan – 2012 Nobel laureate, author of “Red Sorghum” and “The Republic of Wine.”**  
Mo Yan’s works, especially the award‑winning “Red Sorghum” and the satirical “Republic of Wine,” are common clues for contemporary Chinese fiction.

**Scar literature (e.g., “The Class Monitor”).**  
A post‑Cultural‑Revolution movement focusing on the trauma of the era; the term “scar literature” is uniquely associated with Chinese writers.

**“Soul Mountain” – novel sparked by a false cancer diagnosis.**  
The autobiographical journey described in Gao Xingjian’s “Soul Mountain” is often used to cue China through its title and the diagnosis back‑story.

**Pearl S. Buck’s “The Good Earth” – set in China.**  
Although an American author, Buck’s Pulitzer‑winning novel about Chinese peasant life is a classic cultural shortcut to the country.

**Zhongguo – the Mandarin name for China.**  
The Chinese word “Zhongguo” (literally “Middle Kingdom”) appears in many clues as an alternate acceptable answer.

**Red Sorghum – novel and film depicting rural China.**  
Mo Yan’s “Red Sorghum” is a frequently cited work that blends history and myth, serving as a vivid indicator of Chinese literature.

**Trisolaris – the alien civilization from Liu Cixin’s series.**  
The name of the extraterrestrials that contact Earth in “The Three‑Body Problem” is a distinctive sci‑fi element uniquely tied to Chinese authorship.
